title: iHeard STL: Development and first year findings from a local surveillance and rapid response system for addressing COVID-19 and other health misinformation
screen_reason: First-year report of a community misinformation surveillance panel (214 St. Louis residents, weekly mobile surveys). It reports a quantitative share with a denominator: of 1,136 assessable COVID-19 claims that panel members said they had heard in the past seven days, 505 (44%) were classified as misinformation. It also reports how many panel members ever volunteered such a claim (112), giving a self-reported encounter share. The four tracked exposure items are reported only as trend slopes and odds ratios, with the weekly exposure percentages only in a figure.

estimates.country: United States (St. Louis City and St. Louis County, Missouri)
estimates.platform: Weekly mobile-phone survey (open-ended question about COVID-19 information heard in the last seven days, from any source: family, friends, coworkers, social media, other internet, TV or radio)
estimates.measure_type: % of assessable COVID-19 claims that panel members reported hearing in the past seven days that were classified as misinformation
estimates.value_raw: Of the 1,136 assessable claims, 505 (44%) were classified as misinformation
estimates.denominator: 1,136 assessable claims, extracted from 1,449 open-ended responses given by 165 panel members (77% of the 214 enrolled) across 52 weekly surveys; a response was assessable if the claim could be proven or disproven
estimates.definition: Each unique claim reported in a single week was the coding unit. 'Claims were classified as misinformation when they were false or unproven given best available evidence at the time.' Claims that could not be proven or disproven (e.g. 'nothing to report', 'My graduation ceremony required masks') were excluded from the denominator.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation is defined as 'false or inaccurate information'" (citing the American Psychological Association).
estimates.source_quote: Of the 1,136 assessable claims, 505 (44%) were classified as misinformation, with 112 panel members ever providing at least one open-ended response that was classified as misinformation.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two research team members independently coded each open-ended response into one of six exclusive main categories and up to two of 47 non-exclusive sub-categories, using an inductively developed codebook; discrepancies resolved through discussion. Truth judgements were made against peer-reviewed scientific articles, public data, public reports, or news articles from fact-checked news outlets. NO intercoder reliability statistic is reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Claims were assessed for containing misinformation if they could be proven or disproven with peer-reviewed scientific articles, public data, public reports, or news articles from fact-checked news outlets (e.g., New York Times, Washington Post). ... Claims were classified as misinformation when they were false or unproven given best available evidence at the time.
estimates.notes: 505/1,136 = 44.5%; the Results section prints 44% and the Discussion prints 45% ('nearly half of the claims were classified as misinformation (45%)') - a rounding inconsistency inside the paper; I kept the Results figure of 44. CONSTRUCT JUDGEMENT CALL: the denominator is a corpus of claims that RESPONDENTS said they had heard, not a corpus of platform items, so a case exists for coding this EXPOSURE with exposure_type=diet_share ('share of what people encountered that was misinformation'). I coded CONTENT because the unit is the claim and the falsity judgement is researcher coding of item text; borderline=true records the alternative. Note this is a share of what people VOLUNTEERED when asked what else they had heard, so it is a share of salient recalled information, not of a measured information diet. breadth=misleading because the numerator includes claims that are merely 'unproven', which is looser than strict falsity.

estimates.country: United States (St. Louis City and St. Louis County, Missouri)
estimates.measure_type: % of enrolled panel members who, at any point in the year, spontaneously reported hearing at least one COVID-19 claim that was classified as misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 112 panel members ever providing at least one open-ended response that was classified as misinformation, of 214 enrolled
estimates.denominator: 214 panel members enrolled between 23 August 2021 and 21 August 2022 (convenience panel of St. Louis City/County residents and workers, deliberately over-recruiting Black or African American residents and front-line workers)
estimates.definition: A panel member counted in the numerator if at least one of the claims they volunteered, in the weekly open-ended question asking what other COVID-19 information they had heard in the last seven days, was coded by the research team as misinformation.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation is defined as 'false or inaccurate information'".
estimates.source_quote: Of the 1,136 assessable claims, 505 (44%) were classified as misinformation, with 112 panel members ever providing at least one open-ended response that was classified as misinformation.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Open-ended response analysis' (p. 8) and 'Participants and response rates' (p. 6); Table 2
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-reported encounter: panel members volunteered, in a weekly open-ended question, the COVID-19 information they had heard in the last seven days. The FALSITY judgement on those volunteered claims was made by two research team members coding independently against peer-reviewed evidence, public data and fact-checked news outlets, with disagreements resolved by discussion and no reliability statistic reported. ground_truth is recorded as self_report because the exposure event is respondent-reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Across 52 weekly surveys, 165 different panel members (77% of total enrolled) provided 1,449 open-ended responses about other COVID-19 information they had heard in the last week. ... it currently relies on a convenience sample of panel members, which may affect the generalizability of surveillance results. Women and vaccinated individuals are over-represented in our panel, and we intentionally over-recruited Black and African American individuals.
estimates.notes: DERIVED, NOT STATED: 52.3% is 112/214, an exact part/whole share of two verbatim counts (R8-legal), but the authors never express it as a percentage. TREAT WITH CARE: this is UNPROMPTED reporting - a member is counted only if they volunteered a misinformation claim in the free-text box, over a 52-week window - so it is a lower bound on exposure and is NOT comparable to survey items that ask directly 'have you seen misinformation about X'. The alternative denominator is the 165 members who gave any open-ended response (112/165 = 67.9%). The panel is a convenience sample that deliberately over-recruited Black/African American residents and front-line workers and is 85% fully vaccinated, so it is not a general-population estimate. An adjudicator may reasonably drop this row.

missed_or_uncertain: The paper's PRIMARY exposure measure could NOT be extracted: weekly exposure to the four tracked misinformation items (VaxFail, VaxDanger, KidMask, Ivermectin) is reported only as (a) regression slopes - average weekly declines of -8.1% (KidMask), -3.3% (VaxFail), -2.7% (VaxDanger) and -2.6% (Ivermectin) - and (b) Fig 2, a plot of weekly exposure and belief. No level (a share of panel members exposed in a given week or over the year) appears anywhere in the text, so no RECALL row for these items is possible; the only quantitative anchor is the item-retirement rule ('we removed items when <15% of panel members reported hearing the item for at least three consecutive weeks'), which is a threshold, not an estimate. Also not extracted: (1) all odds ratios for first exposure and first belief by subgroup (Table 3; e.g. Black vs white panel members OR=3.4 for VaxDanger exposure, OR=17.1 for VaxDanger belief) - relative measures with no underlying shares printed (raw counts are in supplementary S4 Table, not in this text); (2) belief measures generally - belief in false claims is explicitly outside this review's scope; (3) category shares of the 505 misinformation claims (vaccine 257, 52%; general 162, 33%; disease 50, 10%; virus 22, 4%; healthcare 7, 1%; booster 78, 9%; variants 68, 8%) - within-misinformation topical breakdowns, not prevalence; (4) '488 (43%)' of all assessable claims in the 'vaccine' main category - a topical share, not a falsity share; (5) system-use metrics (15,939 dashboard views, 611 (4%) click-throughs, alert view rate mean 32.5%, engagement rate mean 13.3%) and survey response rates (mean 88.8%, 6,605 of 7,512 surveys completed) - operational, not misinformation prevalence; (6) the '34% of states' figure from reference [8] - cited from elsewhere, excluded by R8. Note also that the abstract reports the mean weekly response rate as 88.3% +/- 6% while the Results give 88.8% +/- 4.8%.

rob.design: Prospective community-panel surveillance, first year (23 Aug 2021 - 21 Aug 2022). Sampling frame: convenience panel of 214 adults recruited through community partners and a research registry in St. Louis City/County, Missouri, deliberately targeting areas with a higher proportion of Black or African American residents and aiming for a 50/50 mix of community members and front-line workers; eligibility = 18+, resident or worker in St. Louis City/County, mobile phone with internet. Panel accrued over the year, so early weeks had <=12 members and were dropped from trend analyses. Response: weekly surveys texted every Sunday, closing after 48 hours; weekly response rates 72.5%-100%, mean 88.8% +/- 4.8% (abstract says 88.3% +/- 6%); 7,512 surveys sent, 6,605 completed; incentives $10 baseline + $5 per weekly survey. Measures: 45 different misinformation items across the year, 5-10 per week, chosen from misinformation-tracking sites (CDC vaccine-confidence reports, Public Health Communication Collaborative alerts, Google FactCheck) and from panel members' own open-ended reports (21 of the 45 originated this way); each item followed immediately by accurate information, which the authors note may attenuate later responses (hence their 'first exposure'/'first belief' variables). Coding of open-ended claims: two independent coders, inductive codebook, discussion to resolve; no reliability statistic. English-language surveys only. Author-declared limitations: convenience sample, over-representation of women and vaccinated people, small numbers giving imprecise subgroup estimates, no multivariable models, non-English communities missed.
